{"id": "b6c98ad0-4ec0-44eb-8ca9-40eb0f5885c0", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Anyone on our team can change the system prompt and deploy it. What is the minimum we should put in place so a quality regression cannot reach production?", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "bee8268d-a354-49c8-9ce7-5778e729a494", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I'm assuming this is your own LLM application's prompt. If you meant something else, tell me and I'll adjust.

The minimum is three controls: no deploy path that skips the checks, an automated eval gate that blocks regressions, and a fast rollback. Staged rollout and review rules come after that.

## The minimum

**1. One deploy path, with no bypass**
- Keep the prompt in version control as a versioned artifact, and deploy it only through a pipeline.
- Remove direct edit and deploy permissions for individuals, including console and API access. If anyone can skip the pipeline, nothing else on this list matters.
- Require a second reviewer who isn't the author. Use code owners for the prompt files so changes get a reviewer who knows the behavior.

**2. An eval gate that blocks the merge or deploy**
- Build a golden dataset of representative inputs, plus every past production failure. Start with 50–200 cases and add one each time something breaks.
- Run the candidate prompt and the current production prompt on the same dataset, with the same model version, parameters and tools. Pin the model version so a model update can't change results unnoticed.
- Fail the pipeline if the candidate scores below production beyond a set tolerance. Use a regression threshold relative to the current baseline, not only an absolute score.
- Include hard checks that don't depend on an LLM judge: output format and schema, refusal and safety cases, required or forbidden content, and tool-call correctness.
- Outputs are nondeterministic, so run each case several times, or use a tolerance band, to avoid flaky gates.
- If you use an LLM judge for quality scoring, spot-check it against human labels, or it becomes a blind spot.

**3. Fast, tested rollback**
- Keep prompt versions immutable and reference them by version ID.
- Make rollback a single action, such as repointing an alias to the previous version, that doesn't need a new review cycle.
- Practice it once so you know it works.

## Next, once those are in place
- **Staged rollout:** use shadow traffic, or a canary of 5–10%, before going to 100%. Compare online signals such as error rate, user feedback, escalation or retry rate, and latency or token cost.
- **Auto-rollback:** trigger it when those online metrics cross a threshold.
- **Audit trail:** record who changed what, when, and which eval results it passed.
- **Scheduled evals:** run the golden set against production regularly. This catches drift from model or dependency changes that no one deployed.

## Why the eval gate matters most
Review alone doesn't catch prompt regressions. A prompt change that looks harmless to a reviewer can quietly break an edge case, and only a test run shows it. Requiring review without an eval gate gives a false sense of safety. An eval gate with no review still catches most regressions. The gate is the one control you can't skip.

If you tell me where the prompt is stored and deployed (for example Bedrock Prompt Management, a config file in a repo, or a parameter store), I can suggest how to wire in the gate and restrict the deploy path. I can also check the IAM and pipeline setup in your associated AWS accounts for who can currently deploy changes.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
